definition: Biomedical text mining (including biomedical natural language processing or BioNLP) refers to the methods and study of how text mining may be applied to texts and literature of the biomedical domain.
details: As a field of research, biomedical text mining incorporates ideas from natural language processing, bioinformatics, medical informatics and computational linguistics. The strategies in this field have been applied to the biomedical literature available through services such as PubMed. In recent years, the scientific literature has shifted to electronic publishing but the volume of information available can be overwhelming. This revolution of publishing has caused a high demand for text mining techniques. Text mining offers information retrieval (IR) and entity recognition (ER). IR allows the retrieval of relevant papers according to the topic of interest, e.g. through PubMed. ER is practiced when certain biological terms are recognized (e.g. proteins or genes) for further processing.

explainer.lead: Biomedical text mining helps researchers find useful papers and spot biological terms such as gene and protein names in a fast-growing literature. It matters because electronic publishing has made far more information available than people can comfortably read on their own.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a library with more new science papers arriving than anyone could ever read. A helpful assistant could fetch the papers about your question and highlight important words, such as the names of genes and proteins. Biomedical text mining teaches computers to do that kind of finding and highlighting.
tiers.practitioner: A typical setup combines information retrieval over biomedical literature, often through services such as PubMed, with entity recognition for gene and protein terms. Retrieval narrows the document set, while recognition identifies biological terms for downstream processing. Treating retrieval and recognition as interchangeable can obscure which part of the pipeline needs work, and the volume of electronic literature makes manual review impractical.
tiers.paperLevel: Biomedical text mining is the application of text-mining methods to biomedical texts and literature, drawing on natural language processing, bioinformatics, medical informatics, and computational linguistics. A basic workflow is topic query -> information retrieval -> relevant papers, followed by text -> entity recognition -> biological terms such as genes or proteins for further processing. A central practical constraint is scale: electronic publishing produces a volume of information that can overwhelm researchers.

explainer.example: A researcher interested in a biological topic uses PubMed to retrieve relevant papers. Entity recognition then marks gene and protein names in those papers, producing identified biological terms for further processing instead of requiring the researcher to locate every mention by hand.

explainer.intuition: Reading every relevant biomedical paper is increasingly difficult, so computers can first narrow the reading list and then mark important biological terms. Search finds the documents; entity recognition finds things such as genes and proteins inside them.
howItWorks: Start with biomedical texts, such as literature available through PubMed.
Use information retrieval to find papers relevant to a topic of interest.
Apply entity recognition to identify biological terms, including gene and protein names.
Pass the recognized terms on for further processing.
explainer.whyItMatters: Electronic publishing has made the biomedical literature so large that its volume can be overwhelming. Text mining helps researchers retrieve relevant papers and extract useful biological terms from them.
misconceptions: It is not just document search: entity recognition can also identify genes, proteins, and other biological terms in text.
Information retrieval and entity recognition are different tasks: retrieval finds relevant papers, while recognition finds terms within text.
It is not limited to one discipline: it draws on natural language processing, bioinformatics, medical informatics, and computational linguistics.
